description: We are Systems Engineering students from Universidad Gerardo Barrios (San Miguel, El Salvador), passionate about using satellite data to tackle real environmental problems. Wildfires and agricultural burning affect our region every year, so this challenge feels personal to us.
summary: FireCal is a web app that turns 26 years of NASA FIRMS active-fire detections into one consistent burning-activity calendar for Central America. MODIS (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012) cannot be compared directly: over the same land, VIIRS reports about 4.7 times more detections, so joining their records makes 2012 look like a fire explosion that never happened. We harmonized both sensors by letting six models compete under leave-one-year-out validation; the winning ensemble cuts the error by 56% compared with a single conversion factor. The result is a month-by-month calendar from November 2000 to October 2026 for any country, drawn area or point, with a simple alert level for fire responders, a detailed view for analysts, and downloadable CSV data and PDF reports. Knowing when and where burning is unusual helps teams anticipate critical periods and plan monitoring and response.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

FireCal answers three questions for any area in Central America (Belize, Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, Nicaragua, Costa Rica and Panama): which months concentrate the most fires, which years had the most burning, and whether the latest month is unusual compared with the same month in past years. Users pick an area by country, by drawing a rectangle or polygon on the map, or by entering a point and a radius, and can choose the period and the historical reference years.

- Responder view: an alert level (Normal, Elevated, High, Extreme) for the latest month with a plain-language explanation, the peak month of the fire season, the most active year, a 10-year calendar where any month can be opened for details, and one-click PDF report and CSV download. Months with zero detections show "No detections" instead of a level. Works on phones.

- Analyst view: the full 2001-2026 calendar with harmonized, raw MODIS and raw VIIRS values, monthly anomalies against the historical median, a side-by-side comparison of two areas, and the full method validation.

HOW IT WORKS

- Data: NASA FIRMS yearly country archives (2000-2025) plus the FIRMS area API for January-October 2026: 2,687,846 hotspots (719,173 MODIS and 1,968,673 VIIRS S-NPP), November 2000 to October 2026.

- Cleaning: detections are filtered by confidence and type. A DBSCAN clustering step removes 275 persistent heat sources such as active volcanoes and industrial sites (1.4% of the quality-filtered detections).

- Harmonization: on a 0.25-degree grid (840 cells x 312 months), six methods compete to predict VIIRS counts from MODIS over the 2012-2025 overlap: one global ratio, one ratio per calendar month, a per-cell ratio with empirical-Bayes shrinkage, Poisson regression, gradient boosting, and an ensemble of empirical Bayes and gradient boosting. Months before mid-2002, when only the Terra satellite flew, use a separate Terra-only model.

- Validation: leave-one-year-out cross-validation; each year from 2012 to 2025 is hidden, predicted from MODIS and checked against real VIIRS. The ensemble wins: mean absolute error of 146 detections per country-month (R2 0.987, bias -0.7%) versus 334 for a single ratio, a 56% reduction. Months before 2012 carry a likely range derived from the validation errors.

- Alerts: each month is ranked against the same calendar month in the reference years (75th, 90th and 97.5th percentiles); months with fewer than 5 detections are never flagged.

BENEFITS

- One sensor-independent record that keeps 26 years comparable and stays useful as MODIS retires and VIIRS continues.

- Fast, plain-language answers for responders, with the scientific detail and uncertainty available for analysts.

- Accessible design: color-blind-safe colors, levels shown with color, icon and text, keyboard navigation, screen-reader labels, English and Spanish, mobile support.

- Open and free: open-source code, free hosting, and downloadable data.

INTENDED IMPACT

We want fire managers in Central America to have an always-current view of when and where burning is unusual, so they can anticipate critical periods and plan monitoring and response. Next steps: a daily view of detections, automatic monthly updates with near-real-time data, the NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 VIIRS sensors, and the same pipeline for other regions.

TOOLS

Python 3.12 (pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn, FastAPI, fpdf2), React and TypeScript (Vite, Leaflet, Apache ECharts), pytest and Vitest, Docker, Render (API), Vercel (web app), GitHub Actions.

Source code: https://github.com/LudwinS/firecal-space-apps-2026

Use of AI: we used Claude (Anthropic) as a coding assistant under the team's direction, as described in the repository README.
